newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi may offer to quit over Albania vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi may offer to quit over Albania vote.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi was ready to offer his resignation later on Wednesday as a final gambit to win parliamentary backing for the deployment of a security force for Albania, newspapers reported.
Prodi was seen leaving President Oscar Luigi Scalforo's office shortly before he was due to open a debate in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) on the mission.
It was not immediately clear what the two men had talked about. Scalfaro is the ultimate arbiter in Italian politics.
Political commentators said they thought Prodi would retain power, despite any resignation offer, but said his 11-month old administration had been seriously wounded by the crisis.
"The government hangs by a thread," Corriere della Sera newspaper said in a front page headline.

The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) was due to vote on the Italian-led mission to Albania later on Wednesday. Prodi is now looking for support from the opposition Freedom Alliance bloc after a hard-left political ally refused to back the operation.
In exchange for opposition backing, Prodi was set to place the future of his minority centre-left government on the line by offering his resignation to Scalfaro.

The Minister for Parliamentary Affairs, Giorgio Bogi, told reporters Prodi would make "an important announcement" in parliament later on Wednesday. The prime minister is scheduled to speak at midday (1000 GMT).

The political impasse has been sparked by the refusal of Communist Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house, to back the multinational force, which it sees as a neocolonial venture.
Albania was occupied by Fascist Italy 58 years ago this week.

But Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said on Wednesday he did not want the issue to lead to the fall of Prodi. "We have always said that a 'no' for the Albania mission would not lead to (the government) falling," Bertinotti told reporters.
If Prodi were to offer his resignation, Scalfaro would almost certainly ask him to return to parliament and seek a confidence motion.
"If the government calls a confidence vote that has nothing to do with the Albania mission, then we'll vote 'yes,'" Bertinotti said.
The split over the 6,000-strong Albania force, which is due to start deploying next week to protect humanitarian relief for the small Balkan state, has dealt a serious blow to Prodi.

"The government is lost in uncertainty and error," the left-leaning daily La Repubblica wrote on Wednesday, adding that if Prodi survived: "The government would be left with the task, or rather the miracle, of resurrecting itself."

The government comfortably won a first vote on the Albanian mission on Tuesday in the upper house (Senate), where it holds a clear majority. A vote in the lower house is due at around eight p.m. (1800 GMT).

The Freedom Alliance, led by former premier Silvio Berlusconi, supports the Albania force but -- sensing an opportunity to embarrass Prodi -- said on Tuesday it would not vote for the government motion and instead proposed its own, similar motion which it called on Prodi to back.

The government, unwilling to submit to the humiliation of needing an opposition motion to ratify the U.N.-approved Albania mission, turned down that demand and instead asked the centre-right to vote for a joint document.
Rocco Buttiglione, head of the small CDU party within the Freedom Alliance, told reporters the bloc would probably approve such a motion if Prodi promised to resign.

Italy is expected to contribute 2,500 troops to the Albanian operation, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. It is the first time Italy has led such a multi-national operation.
